newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Common hatreds, loyalties bind Zairean rebel force.
newsitem.headline: Common hatreds, loyalties bind Zairean rebel force.

text.p: Hatred of ailing and absent President Mobutu Sese Seko as well as deep-rooted, personal and secretive links with various governments in the region all combine to unite an alliance of rebels fighting in Zaire.

Ties in Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL), which now occupies over a fifth of Zaire, hinge on ethnicity, ideology and personal friendship, diplomats and rebel insiders say.
Kabila says he wants to take over Africa's third largest country and has given himself a June deadline.

The core of Kabila's fighting force is ethnic Tutsi or the Banyamulenge -- ancestral Tutsis who migrated from Rwanda more than 200 years ago and settled in Zaire's mulenge mountains near eastern town of Uvira.
"We had been preparing for years and when we found out that the Banyamulenge were themselves preparing for war it made sense that we should join forces," said an ally of Kabila.

Rwanda denies involvement in the civil war but western intelligence sources say serving members of Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated army are fighting alongside Kabila's force -- Africa's latest guerrilla group.
"Demobilised" Ugandan troops hired on contract also make up a part of the rebel force, whose field commanders are a mixture of foreigners and Zaireans.
Thousands of youths scenting victory have been given training, but have yet to make a major battlefront contribution.

Even some "Katangese Tigers" who fought separatist rebellions for their southern Shaba region in the 1960s and 1970s have not been discouraged from joining the fighting force, even though they recently sided with Mobutu.

Other recruits to the rebel cause have been more of a problem than a help. Teenage Mai Mai warriors, who believe magic makes them invisible, turned their guns on the rest of the Alliance only weeks after joining the rebellion in October.

Kabila is a non-Tutsi and native of mineral-rich Shaba province. He has spent time in exile mainly in Tanzania, then a base for African leaders and where he met and became friends with Yoweri Museveni, and also in Uganda and Rwanda.
Kabila has battled Mobutu since he was in his 20s and now heads an alliance as multi-coloured as the military force.

"Democracy, Justice and Unity," the AFDL motto, joins would- be communists and followers of murdered independence Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba with western-inspired free-marketeers educated in exile.
The link from Museveni to Rwandan strongman Major-General Paul Kagame to the Banyamulenge is at the heart of claims by Zaire that Rwanda and Uganda back the rebellion.

The Banyamulenge, a minority of 400,000 or less, had been training for months to deal with a threat of expulsion to their ancestral homeland, and the arrival of over a million Hutu refugees after Rwanda's 1994 genocide.

Fearing reprisals for the mass killing of 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus the refugees fled to Zaire, which under Mobutu was closely allied to the former Hutu government. Among the refugees were former soldiers and militiamen who organised the massacres and vowed to return by force of arms.
Now they have either been forced home or driven deep into Zaire's jungle where they no longer pose a security threat to Rwanda's Tutsi-led army.
The AFDL push has also benefitted Uganda's Museveni, who has driven rebel factions from their bases in the remote border region between the two countries.
